claim: Tunicamycin (TM) blocks N-linked glycosylation, an ER-specific protein modification.
source: TM blocks N-linked glycosylation, an ER-specific protein modification.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text as a known property of tunicamycin.

claim: Tunicamycin has few known off-target effects and most prominently targets the kidneys and the liver.
source: It has few known off-target effects, most prominently targets the kidneys and the liver, and is not lethal in wild-type animals at even relatively high doses (Foufelle and Fromenty, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Foufelle and Fromenty, 2016.

claim: Tunicamycin is not lethal in wild-type animals at even relatively high doses.
source: It has few known off-target effects, most prominently targets the kidneys and the liver, and is not lethal in wild-type animals at even relatively high doses (Foufelle and Fromenty, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Foufelle and Fromenty, 2016.

claim: The effects of tunicamycin on the liver can be mimicked by other agents that elicit ER stress in that organ.
source: Its effects on the liver can also be mimicked, albeit less readily, by other agents that elicit ER stress in that organ (Rutkowski et al., 2008; Chikka et al., 2013), further justifying its use here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rutkowski et al., 2008 and Chikka et al., 2013.

claim: Doses of TM below 0.1 mg/kg are capable of eliciting attenuated UPR activation.
source: Using qRT-PCR to detect changes in expression of the UPR sentinel genes Hspa5 (encoding BiP) and Ddit3 (encoding CHOP), we found that doses of TM below 0.1 mg/kg were capable of eliciting attenuated UPR activation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Acute treatment (8 hr) with 0.025 mg/kg TM is sufficient to lead to upregulation of both BiP and CHOP at the protein level.
source: As expected, acute treatment (8 hr) with this dose of TM was sufficient to lead to upregulation of both BiP and CHOP at the protein level (Figure 1B), although for CHOP this induction was much more modest than commonly elicited by higher doses of TM.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CHOP induction by 0.025 mg/kg TM is much more modest than commonly elicited by higher doses of TM.
source: As expected, acute treatment (8 hr) with this dose of TM was sufficient to lead to upregulation of both BiP and CHOP at the protein level (Figure 1B), although for CHOP this induction was much more modest than commonly elicited by higher doses of TM.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B and comparison to known effects of higher doses.

claim: The predominant acute effect of TM on the liver is the formation of intracellular vacuoles in hepatocytes that correspond to accumulated lipid droplets.
source: The predominant acute effect of TM on the liver, as revealed by hematoxylin and eosin staining, was the formation of intracellular vacuoles in hepatocytes (Figure 1D) that correspond to accumulated lipid droplets resulting from impaired lipid metabolism (Rutkowski et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 1D and a citation to Rutkowski et al., 2008.

claim: Intracellular vacuoles in hepatocytes result from impaired lipid metabolism.
source: The predominant acute effect of TM on the liver, as revealed by hematoxylin and eosin staining, was the formation of intracellular vacuoles in hepatocytes (Figure 1D) that correspond to accumulated lipid droplets resulting from impaired lipid metabolism (Rutkowski et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rutkowski et al., 2008.

claim: Persistent underglycosylation of TRAPα at day five confirms that tunicamycin remained active upon repeated dosing.
source: However, persistent underglycosylation of the ER-resident glycoprotrein TRAPα at day five confirmed that the drug remained active upon repeated dosing (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: BiP upregulation persists throughout the chronic stress time-course.
source: Immunoblotting showed that BiP upregulation persisted throughout the time-course (Figure 1F), as did upregulation of the ER chaperone GRP94 (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GRP94 upregulation persists throughout the chronic stress time-course.
source: Immunoblotting showed that BiP upregulation persisted throughout the time-course (Figure 1F), as did upregulation of the ER chaperone GRP94 (not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text but data is not shown.

claim: Upregulation of CHOP protein was lost by D1-24h and remained mostly undetectable in animals treated for 5 days.
source: In contrast, and consistent with the effects of chronic stress on cultured cells (Rutkowski et al., 2006), upregulation of the highly labile CHOP protein was lost even by D1-24h, and remained mostly undetectable in animals treated for 5 days (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1F and a citation to Rutkowski et al., 2006.

claim: ADRP expression correlates with lipid droplet content.
source: We also monitored the lipid droplet marker protein ADRP, the expression of which correlates with lipid droplet content.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ADRP.

claim: ADRP expression was elevated in animals treated for one day, but returned to basal levels in animals treated for five days.
source: Consistent with histological data (Figure 1D), ADRP expression—and therefore intracellular lipid accumulation—was elevated in animals treated for one day, but returned to basal levels in animals treated for five days (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1F and histological data in Figure 1D.

claim: Ddit3 mRNA is upregulated by acute stress but its expression returns to basal levels by 24 hr and remains at similar levels at every subsequent time point, even after 18d of repeated treatment.
source: Despite Ddit3 mRNA being upregulated by acute stress (Figure 1A), its expression returned to basal levels by 24 hr (D1-24h) and remained at similar levels at every subsequent time point, even after 18d of repeated treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 1A and 2A.

claim: Hspa5 mRNA levels were significantly diminished below basal levels by 24 hr and continued to diminish further through the first five days, remaining suppressed thereafter.
source: Surprisingly, however, Hspa5 mRNA levels—while elevated by acute stress (Figure 1A)—were significantly diminished below basal levels by 24 hr and continued to diminish further through the first five days, remaining suppressed thereafter (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 1A and 2A.

claim: The suppression of Hspa5 mRNA reflects total Hspa5 mRNA levels rather than alternate splicing.
source: Similar results were obtained using qRT-PCR primers bridging a separate pair of exons in Hspa5 mRNA, demonstrating that this suppression reflected total Hspa5 mRNA levels rather than alternate splicing (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data using alternate primers shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Herpud1 and Hsp90b1 mRNAs display similar downregulation to Hspa5 in the chronic condition.
source: These included mRNAs encoding the ER-associated degradation factor Herpud1 and Hsp90b1 (encoding the ER chaperone GRP94). (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Metabolic genes that are suppressed by acute ER stress in the liver are not significantly suppressed in the chronic condition.
source: While each of these was downregulated in the acute condition as expected (not shown), none was significantly suppressed in the chronic condition (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The suppression of Hspa5 and other mRNAs during chronic ER stress is mechanistically distinct from the pathways that suppress metabolic gene expression during acute stress.
source: This finding provides evidence that the suppression of Hspa5 and other mRNAs during chronic ER stress is mechanistically distinct from the pathways that suppress metabolic gene expression during acute stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential behavior of these gene sets in chronic vs acute stress.

claim: Hspa5, Herpud1, and Hsp90b1 have been identified as targets of the ATF6α pathway of the UPR.
source: One of the commonalities among the genes that were suppressed below basal levels (Hspa5, Herpud1, Hsp90b1) is that each has been identified as a target of the ATF6α pathway of the UPR (Yoshida et al., 2001; Yamamoto et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 2001; Yamamoto et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2007.

claim: Acute stress (8 hr treatment with 0.025 mg/kg TM) leads to elevated expression of ATF4, XBP1spl and ATF6αcl in liver nuclei.
source: As a positive control, acute stress (8 hr treatment with 0.025 mg/kg TM as in Figure 1A) led to elevated expression of ATF4, XBP1spl and ATF6αcl; however, all three were undetectable in the chronic condition (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data from nuclear extracts shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ATF4, XBP1spl and ATF6αcl are undetectable in liver nuclei in the chronic condition.
source: As a positive control, acute stress (8 hr treatment with 0.025 mg/kg TM as in Figure 1A) led to elevated expression of ATF4, XBP1spl and ATF6αcl; however, all three were undetectable in the chronic condition (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data from nuclear extracts shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ATF6α binds to the Hspa5 promoter following 8 hr of treatment with TM.
source: For this experiment, the Hspa5 promoter was recovered by an ATF6α antibody following 8 hr of treatment served as expected (Yoshida et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data and a citation to Yoshida et al., 1998.

claim: No ATF6α binding above background is detected at the Hspa5 promoter in the chronic condition.
source: In contrast, no ATF6α binding above background was detected in the chronic condition (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RNA Polymerase 2 is poised at the Hspa5 promoter and this binding is unaffected by the presence or absence of ER stress.
source: As expected, Pol2 was recovered near the Hspa5 transcriptional start site (−215 to +0), and this binding was unaffected by the presence or absence of ER stress (Figure 3C). This binding reflects Pol2 that is poised at the Hspa5 promoter waiting to be engaged during the transcriptional activation process (Muse et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C and a citation to Muse et al., 2007.

claim: Pol2 is abundantly recovered from the body of the Hspa5 locus during acute stress but this binding is completely lost in the chronic condition.
source: In contrast, while Pol2 was abundantly recovered from the body of the Hspa5 locus during acute stress (Intron 7, or +2727 to +2906, which reflects elongating polymerase), this binding was completely lost in the chronic condition (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The basal expression of Hspa5 in animals lacking ATF6α is reduced by approximately 50 percent relative to wild-type animals.
source: Confirming this prediction, we found that the basal expression of Hspa5 in animals lacking ATF6α was reduced by approximately 50 percent relative to wild-type animals, and that chronic stress then had no further effect on Hspa5 expression (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from Atf6-/- mice shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Chronic stress has no further effect on Hspa5 expression in animals lacking ATF6α.
source: Confirming this prediction, we found that the basal expression of Hspa5 in animals lacking ATF6α was reduced by approximately 50 percent relative to wild-type animals, and that chronic stress then had no further effect on Hspa5 expression (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from Atf6-/- mice shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Loss of ATF6α alone is sufficient to mimic chronic stress treatment with respect to Hspa5 expression.
source: Thus, loss of ATF6α alone was sufficient to mimic chronic stress treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that Atf6-/- mice have suppressed Hspa5 expression similar to chronic stress.

claim: The ATF6α pathway of the UPR is engaged in the liver absent exogenous stress.
source: From these data, we conclude that at least the ATF6α pathway of the UPR is engaged in the liver absent exogenous stress, and that even this basal component can be inhibited upon chronic stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Atf6-/- mice have reduced basal Hspa5 expression.

claim: The basal component of ATF6α activity can be inhibited upon chronic stress.
source: From these data, we conclude that at least the ATF6α pathway of the UPR is engaged in the liver absent exogenous stress, and that even this basal component can be inhibited upon chronic stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing suppression of Hspa5 in chronic stress conditions.

claim: The UPR remains essentially as stress-responsive on the fifth day as on the first day of TM treatment.
source: This experiment demonstrated that the UPR remained essentially as stress-responsive on the fifth day as on the first; splicing of Xbp1 8 hr after the first injection and 8 hr after the fifth were induced to comparable levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by Xbp1 splicing data comparing D1-8h and D5-8h timepoints.

claim: Splicing of Xbp1 8 hr after the first injection and 8 hr after the fifth injection are induced to comparable levels.
source: This experiment demonstrated that the UPR remained essentially as stress-responsive on the fifth day as on the first; splicing of Xbp1 8 hr after the first injection and 8 hr after the fifth were induced to comparable levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by Xbp1 splicing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The deactivation of Xbp1 splicing activity of IRE1α proceeds more rapidly on day five than on day 1.
source: Yet the deactivation of the UPR, or at least the Xbp1 splicing activity of IRE1α, proceeded more rapidly on day five than on day 1; substantial Xbp1 splicing was seen 14 hr after the first injection but not 14 hr after the fifth (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Xbp1 splicing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Repeated TM treatment continues to induce short-term lipid dysregulation.
source: Supporting the idea that the UPR remained responsive, repeated TM treatment continued to induce short-term lipid dysregulation, as evidenced by abundant cytoplasmic vacuoles in D5-8h livers (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hspa5 expression is well-induced after both the first and fifth TM treatments, but its attenuation proceeds more rapidly in the chronic condition.
source: We also monitored Hspa5 mRNA expression over a similar time course, and found that its expression mirrored this pattern—namely, that Hspa5 expression was well-induced after both treatments, but that its attenuation proceeded more rapidly in the chronic condition (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Hsp90b1 (encoding GRP94) mRNA expression is well-induced after both the first and fifth TM treatments, but its attenuation proceeds more rapidly in the chronic condition.
source: Similar results were also obtained for Hsp90b1 (encoding GRP94) mRNA (not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text but data is not shown.

claim: Hspa5 mRNA half-life is 8.2 hr after treatment with TM in primary hepatocytes.
source: However, by monitoring Hspa5 expression after treatment of primary hepatocytes with the transcription inhibitor Actinomycin D, we measured Hspa5 mRNA half-life as 8.2 hr after treatment with TM (Figure 4E), consistent with our previous measurement in MEFs (Rutkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by actinomycin D chase data shown in Figure 4E and a citation to Rutkowski et al., 2006.

claim: Deactivation of the UPR is accompanied by stimulated degradation of Hspa5 mRNA.
source: The simplest explanation for these results is that deactivation of the UPR is accompanied by stimulated degradation of Hspa5 mRNA, for even the loss of Hspa5 that occurs on the first day of treatment (Figure 4D) is too rapid to be accounted for by inhibition of transcription alone.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between the measured mRNA half-life and the observed rate of Hspa5 mRNA decline.

claim: Regulated IRE1-Dependent Decay (RIDD) is the process by which activated IRE1 directly degrades ER-associated mRNAs.
source: A candidate pathway for stimulated degradation of Hspa5 mRNA is Regulated IRE1-Dependent Decay (RIDD), which is the process by which activated IRE1 directly degrades ER-associated mRNAs (Hollien et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hollien et al., 2009.

claim: RIDD is thought to be counter-adaptive, facilitating cell death during severe ER stress.
source: This process is thought to be counter-adaptive, facilitating cell death during severe ER stress (Han et al., 2009; Upton et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Han et al., 2009 and Upton et al., 2012.

claim: RIDD has been implicated in metabolic regulation in the liver.
source: However, it has also been implicated in metabolic regulation in the liver (Cretenet et al., 2010; So et al., 2012), implying that perhaps its function is more nuanced.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cretenet et al., 2010 and So et al., 2012.

claim: Hspa5 has been proposed to be a RIDD target.
source: Hspa5 at least has also been proposed to be a RIDD target, though with unclear functional significance (Han et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Han et al., 2009.

claim: Bloc1s1 is a bona fide RIDD target in MEFs lacking IRE1α, in which its downregulation by ER stress is completely lost.
source: We confirmed that Bloc1s1 is a bona fide RIDD target in MEFs lacking IRE1α, in which its downregulation by ER stress was completely lost (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from Ern1-/- MEFs shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Bloc1s1 expression is reduced in the liver by acute (8 hr) TM treatment.
source: As expected, Bloc1s1 expression was reduced in the liver by acute (8 hr) TM treatment (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Bloc1s1 expression returns to normal levels 24 hr after the first TM treatment, but remains suppressed 24 hr after the fifth treatment.
source: Furthermore, while Bloc1s1 expression returned to normal levels 24 hr after the first TM treatment, it remained suppressed 24 hr after the fifth treatment (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Fn1 is a potential RIDD target in the liver based on microarray data from wild-type and liver-specific Ern1-/- mice treated with TM.
source: Suppression of a RIDD target in the chronic condition was also seen for Fn1, which we found to be a potential RIDD target in the liver based on microarray data from wild-type and liver-specific Ern1-/- (encoding IRE1α) mice treated with TM (Zhang et al., 2011) (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data from Zhang et al., 2011 and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: BiP protein overexpression suppresses Hspa5 mRNA expression.
source: Using primers that detect the 5' UTR of Hspa5 mRNA (and thus amplify only endogenous Hspa5 and not exogenous), we found that, like chronic stress, BiP protein overexpression suppressed Hspa5 mRNA expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from ad-BiP treated mice shown in Figure 5C.

claim: BiP protein overexpression suppresses Hsp90b1 mRNA expression.
source: Similar results were obtained for Hsp90b1, while overexpression had no effect on Ddit3 expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from ad-BiP treated mice shown in Figure 5C.

claim: BiP protein overexpression has no effect on Ddit3 expression.
source: Similar results were obtained for Hsp90b1, while overexpression had no effect on Ddit3 expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from ad-BiP treated mice shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Bloc1s1 expression is suppressed by BiP overexpression.
source: Surprisingly, Bloc1s1 expression was also suppressed under these conditions, again mirroring the chronic condition (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from ad-BiP treated mice shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Treatment with TUDCA reduces stress-induced expression of Hspa5, Hsp90b1, and Ddit3 approximately two-fold or more.
source: We found that treating mice with the pharmacological chaperone TUDCA (Ozcan et al., 2006)—which reduced upregulation of ER stress markers by TM approximately 2-fold—had no effect on its own on any UPR gene tested (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from TUDCA-treated mice shown in Figure 5E and a citation to Ozcan et al., 2006.

claim: TUDCA treatment has no effect on basal Hspa5 expression.
source: We found that treating mice with the pharmacological chaperone TUDCA (Ozcan et al., 2006)—which reduced upregulation of ER stress markers by TM approximately 2-fold—had no effect on its own on any UPR gene tested (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from TUDCA-treated mice shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Improved ER protein folding capacity is not sufficient to suppress Hspa5 expression.
source: These data show that improved ER protein folding capacity was not sufficient to suppress Hspa5 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the TUDCA data showing no effect on basal Hspa5 expression.

claim: Feeding elicits ER stress in mouse livers.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Oyadomari et al., 2008; Pfaffenbach et al., 2010), we found that feeding elicited ER stress in mouse livers (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A and citations to Oyadomari et al., 2008 and Pfaffenbach et al., 2010.

claim: Feeding-induced ER stress is much more robust for Hspa5, Hsp90b1, and Xbp1 than for targets of the PERK pathway (Ddit3, Ppp1r15a, and Wars).
source: Interestingly, at least at this timepoint the effect was much more robust for some targets (Hspa5, Hsp90b1, and Xbp1) than others; in fact, targets of the PERK pathway (Ddit3, Ppp1r15a [encoding GADD34], and Wars) were not upregulated to a statistically significant extent under these conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is no difference between the level of ER stress induced by diets containing either high fat or no fat.
source: While it has been proposed that a high fat diet is intrinsically stress-inducing (Ozcan et al., 2004), at least in this instance we found no difference between the level of stress induced by diets containing either high fat or no fat (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data comparing high fat and no fat diets shown in Figure 6A and a citation to Ozcan et al., 2004.

claim: Nutrient intake itself elicits ER stress.
source: This result indicates that nutrient intake itself elicits ER stress, and is consistent with the idea that the stress is driven by increased anabolism (Ozcan et al., 2008) rather than fat per se.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both high fat and no fat diets induce similar ER stress and supported by a citation to Ozcan et al., 2008.

claim: Feeding-induced ER stress is modest compared to that induced by TM.
source: As we speculated, this stress is modest compared to that induced by TM, for which most UPR targets were induced to an extent that was at least an order of magnitude greater than feeding (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing qRT-PCR data from Figure 6A and Figure 6B.

claim: Hspa5 and Hsp90b1 are both significantly suppressed in Lepob/ob and Leprdb/db mice.
source: We observed a similar pattern of gene regulation in these animals as in animals treated with chronic TM; Hspa5 and Hsp90b1 were both significantly suppressed (Figure 6C), while other UPR targets were not suppressed (and, indeed, appeared to be upregulated; Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from obese mice shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Other UPR targets are not suppressed in Lepob/ob and Leprdb/db mice and appear to be upregulated.
source: We observed a similar pattern of gene regulation in these animals as in animals treated with chronic TM; Hspa5 and Hsp90b1 were both significantly suppressed (Figure 6C), while other UPR targets were not suppressed (and, indeed, appeared to be upregulated; Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from obese mice shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Bloc1s1 expression is reduced in Leprdb/db mice and potentially in Lepob/ob mice.
source: In addition, again mirroring the results seen in TM-treated animals, expression of Bloc1s1 was reduced in Leprdb/db mice and potentially in Lepob/ob mice as well, and Fn1 was strongly suppressed in both (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from obese mice shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Fn1 expression is strongly suppressed in both Lepob/ob and Leprdb/db mice.
source: In addition, again mirroring the results seen in TM-treated animals, expression of Bloc1s1 was reduced in Leprdb/db mice and potentially in Lepob/ob mice as well, and Fn1 was strongly suppressed in both (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from obese mice shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Suppression of Hspa5 and Hsp90b1 mRNA expression characterizes both pharmacological and dietary models of chronic stress.
source: These results suggest that suppression of the mRNA expression of Hspa5 and Hsp90b1 characterizes both pharmacological and dietary models of chronic stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar patterns observed in TM-treated and obese mice.

claim: In the basal state, activation of ATF6α contributes to the expression of Hspa5 mRNA.
source: In the basal (i.e., nominally 'unstressed') state, activation of ATF6α contributes to the expression of Hspa5 mRNA. We arrive at this conclusion because expression of Hspa5 was diminished in the absence of ATF6α even without an exogenous stress (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Atf6-/- mice have reduced basal Hspa5 expression.

claim: Normal physiological function in the liver entails periods of UPR activation.
source: This finding implies that normal physiological function in the liver entails periods of UPR activation—perhaps not surprisingly, given that feeding itself activates the UPR (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is inferred from the basal ATF6α activity and the observation that feeding activates the UPR.

claim: BiP is one of the most abundant proteins in the ER lumen.
source: BiP is one of the most abundant proteins in the ER lumen (Gething, 1999), and other non-stress-dependent mechanisms contribute to its basal regulation as well (Resendez et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gething, 1999 and Resendez et al., 1988.

claim: Non-stress-dependent mechanisms contribute to BiP's basal regulation.
source: BiP is one of the most abundant proteins in the ER lumen (Gething, 1999), and other non-stress-dependent mechanisms contribute to its basal regulation as well (Resendez et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Resendez et al., 1988.

claim: Upon exposure to a conventional ER stress, all three limbs of the UPR are activated.
source: Upon exposure to a conventional ER stress, all three limbs of the UPR are activated (Rutkowski et al., 2006), leading to robust production of stress-specific target transcripts such as Ddit3 (Chop), as well as augmentation of transcripts encoding ER chaperones, such as Hspa5 and Hsp90b1 (Grp94).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rutkowski et al., 2006.

claim: CHOP (both mRNA and protein) is naturally labile and readily lost as UPR stress-sensing molecules become deactivated.
source: As the UPR stress-sensing molecules become deactivated, naturally labile factors such as CHOP (both mRNA and protein) are readily lost (Rutkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rutkowski et al., 2006.

claim: ER chaperones such as BiP and GRP94 are long-lived at both the protein and mRNA levels.
source: However, ER chaperones such as BiP and GRP94 are long-lived at both the protein and mRNA levels (Rutkowski et al., 2006), and continued overproduction of these proteins would presumably greatly tax cellular resources and potentially constitute their own burden on the organelle.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rutkowski et al., 2006.

claim: BiP overexpression initiates a negative feedback loop, both suppressing UPR activity and indirectly stimulating the degradation of its own mRNA.
source: Thus, BiP overexpression appears to initiate a negative feedback loop, both suppressing UPR activity (including the basal activity of ATF6α) and also indirectly stimulating the degradation of its own mRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing BiP overexpression suppresses Hspa5 mRNA and ATF6α activity.

claim: During repeated stress, suppression of Hspa5 mRNA constitutes a resetting to a new quasi-stable setpoint for UPR transcriptional regulation.
source: However, during repeated stress, we propose that it constitutes a resetting to a new quasi-stable setpoint for UPR transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the chronic stress data.

claim: Activation of the ER stress sensing molecules requires their dissociation from BiP in both yeast and mammals.
source: One of the founding observations of the UPR field was that activation of the ER stress sensing molecules required their dissociation from BiP in both yeast and mammals (Bertolotti et al., 2000; Shen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bertolotti et al., 2000 and Shen et al., 2002.

claim: Yeast Ire1p can be activated by direct binding to unfolded proteins.
source: However, the suggestion that at least yeast Ire1p can be activated by direct binding to unfolded proteins (Kimata et al., 2004; Gardner and Walter, 2011; Gardner et al., 2013) has cast doubt on this model.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kimata et al., 2004; Gardner and Walter, 2011; Gardner et al., 2013.

claim: The role of BiP binding to UPR stress sensors is to modulate UPR deactivation rather than activation.
source: Our data raise the possibility that perhaps the role of BiP binding is to instead modulate UPR deactivation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data showing BiP's role in chronic stress.

claim: Tunicamycin is capable of disrupting carbohydrate metabolism.
source: While relatively specific in inducing ER stress due to its blockage of N-linked glycosylation, TM also is capable of disrupting carbohydrate metabolism (Olden et al., 1979) and protein palmitoylation (Patterson and Skene, 1995), although whether it does so at the doses used here is unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Olden et al., 1979.

claim: Tunicamycin is capable of disrupting protein palmitoylation.
source: While relatively specific in inducing ER stress due to its blockage of N-linked glycosylation, TM also is capable of disrupting carbohydrate metabolism (Olden et al., 1979) and protein palmitoylation (Patterson and Skene, 1995), although whether it does so at the doses used here is unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patterson and Skene, 1995.

claim: The magnitude of ER stress elicited by feeding is considerably lower than that elicited by tunicamycin.
source: However, as we have demonstrated, the magnitude of ER stress elicited by feeding is considerably lower than that elicited by tunicamycin (Figure 6; also compare Figure 6A with Figure 4D), yet also much more repetitive than the once-daily TM challenge.
evidence: This is supported by comparing qRT-PCR data from feeding experiments and TM experiments.

claim: Atf6 mRNA is significantly downregulated by chronic stress.
source: Along these lines, we observed that Atf6 mRNA is also significantly downregulated by chronic stress, albeit not as robustly as Hspa5 (not shown), raising the possibility of a positive feedback loop for suppressing Hspa5 expression even as BiP protein levels subside.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text but data is not shown.

claim: RIDD might remain active in the chronic condition, even as UPR-dependent transcriptional signaling is shut off.
source: A surprising conclusion from this work is that RIDD might remain active in the chronic condition, even as UPR-dependent transcriptional signaling is shut off.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistent suppression of RIDD targets in the chronic condition.

claim: The purpose of RIDD-mediated clearance of ER-resident proteins might be to help turn the UPR off once stress has been overcome.
source: The purpose of the clearance of ER-resident proteins might not so much be to neuter the organelle and hasten its dysfunction during severe stress (Maurel et al., 2014) as to help turn the response off once stress has been overcome.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of RIDD function based on the chronic stress data and a citation to Maurel et al., 2014.

claim: The dissociation of Xbp1 splicing and RIDD activities occurs to separate activation from deactivation rather than to separate adaptive from apoptotic outputs.
source: They raise the possibility that this dissociation occurs not necessarily to separate adaptive from apoptotic outputs so much as to separate activation from deactivation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of IRE1α activity dissociation.

claim: CHOP promotes cell death during severe stress.
source: Indeed, a parallel can be drawn with the UPR-regulated transcription factor CHOP which, though it clearly promotes cell death during severe stress (Zinszner et al., 1998) also might promote normal cellular function during milder stress both by potentiating the dephosphorylation of eIF2α (Marciniak et al., 2004) and by regulating lipid metabolism (Tyra et al., 2012; Chikka et al., 2013) toward the ultimate improvement of ER function.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zinszner et al., 1998.

claim: CHOP might promote normal cellular function during milder stress by potentiating the dephosphorylation of eIF2α.
source: Indeed, a parallel can be drawn with the UPR-regulated transcription factor CHOP which, though it clearly promotes cell death during severe stress (Zinszner et al., 1998) also might promote normal cellular function during milder stress both by potentiating the dephosphorylation of eIF2α (Marciniak et al., 2004) and by regulating lipid metabolism (Tyra et al., 2012; Chikka et al., 2013) toward the ultimate improvement of ER function.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marciniak et al., 2004.

claim: CHOP might promote normal cellular function during milder stress by regulating lipid metabolism.
source: Indeed, a parallel can be drawn with the UPR-regulated transcription factor CHOP which, though it clearly promotes cell death during severe stress (Zinszner et al., 1998) also might promote normal cellular function during milder stress both by potentiating the dephosphorylation of eIF2α (Marciniak et al., 2004) and by regulating lipid metabolism (Tyra et al., 2012; Chikka et al., 2013) toward the ultimate improvement of ER function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tyra et al., 2012 and Chikka et al., 2013.

claim: Neither MEFs nor cultured hepatocytes show the same suppression of Hspa5 expression as seen in vivo.
source: However, neither MEFs nor even cultured hepatocytes showed the same suppression of Hspa5 expression as seen in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments not shown in detail.

claim: There exist unappreciated factors that influence UPR output in the liver.
source: This discrepancy points to the existence of other as yet unappreciated factors that influence UPR output in the liver.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: Overlaid atop the structural framework of the canonical UPR lie modulatory pathways for altering UPR sensitivity and output.
source: Indeed, it is now becoming clear that, overlaid atop the structural framework of the canonical UPR lie modulatory pathways for altering UPR sensitivity and output, with potential implications for signaling during chronic stress.
evidence: This is stated as emerging knowledge in the field.

claim: S-nitrosylation of IRE1α is a posttranslational modification that can alter UPR output.
source: These include posttranslational modifications either of the stress sensors—such as S-nitrosylation of IRE1α (Yang et al., 2015)—or of ER chaperones, such as ADP ribosylation (Chambers et al., 2012) or AMPylation (Preissler et al., 2015) of BiP.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: ADP ribosylation of BiP is a posttranslational modification that can alter UPR output.
source: These include posttranslational modifications either of the stress sensors—such as S-nitrosylation of IRE1α (Yang et al., 2015)—or of ER chaperones, such as ADP ribosylation (Chambers et al., 2012) or AMPylation (Preissler et al., 2015) of BiP.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chambers et al., 2012.

claim: AMPylation of BiP is a posttranslational modification that can alter UPR output.
source: These include posttranslational modifications either of the stress sensors—such as S-nitrosylation of IRE1α (Yang et al., 2015)—or of ER chaperones, such as ADP ribosylation (Chambers et al., 2012) or AMPylation (Preissler et al., 2015) of BiP.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Preissler et al., 2015.

claim: The UPR has a remarkable capacity to adapt to chronic stress.
source: Finally, our results underscore the remarkable capacity of the UPR to adapt to chronic stress.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: Chronic ER stress is implicated in many chronic diseases.
source: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress is implicated in many chronic diseases, but very little is known about how the unfolded protein response (UPR) responds to persistent ER stress in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Repeated injection of a low dose of tunicamycin experimentally reconstitutes chronic ER stress in the mouse liver.
source: Here, we experimentally reconstituted chronic ER stress in the mouse liver, using repeated injection of a low dose of the ER stressor tunicamycin.
evidence: This is the primary experimental approach described in the abstract.

claim: Chronic ER stress treatment leads to feedback-mediated suppression of mRNAs encoding BiP and GRP94.
source: Paradoxically, this treatment led to feedback-mediated suppression of a select group of mRNAs, including those encoding the ER chaperones BiP and GRP94.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The suppression of BiP and GRP94 mRNAs during chronic stress is due to both silencing of the ATF6α pathway and enhancement of mRNA degradation.
source: This suppression was due to both silencing of the ATF6α pathway of UPR-dependent transcription and enhancement of mRNA degradation, possibly via regulated IRE1-dependent decay (RIDD).
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The suppression of BiP mRNA is phenocopied by ectopic overexpression of BiP protein.
source: The suppression of mRNA encoding BiP was phenocopied by ectopic overexpression of BiP protein, and was also observed in obese mice.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The suppression of BiP mRNA is observed in obese mice.
source: The suppression of mRNA encoding BiP was phenocopied by ectopic overexpression of BiP protein, and was also observed in obese mice.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Persistent cycles of UPR activation and deactivation create an altered, quasi-stable setpoint for UPR-dependent transcriptional regulation.
source: Our findings suggest that persistent cycles of UPR activation and deactivation create an altered, quasi-stable setpoint for UPR-dependent transcriptional regulation—an outcome that could be relevant to conditions such as metabolic syndrome.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: The altered UPR setpoint could be relevant to conditions such as metabolic syndrome.
source: Our findings suggest that persistent cycles of UPR activation and deactivation create an altered, quasi-stable setpoint for UPR-dependent transcriptional regulation—an outcome that could be relevant to conditions such as metabolic syndrome.
evidence: This is a speculative implication stated in the abstract.
